findings.description: AC-006 promises that a rule never replaces a word fragment, but U+200C ZWNJ and U+200D ZWJ (General_Category Cf) are not word characters. In Persian and Urdu, ZWNJ joins morphemes inside one word (for example the continuous prefix in 'می‌خواهم'), so a rule for 'می' replaces that prefix inside the verb; Unicode word segmentation (UAX #29 WB4) treats both joiners as word-internal.
findings.suggestion: Either add Join_Control (ZWNJ, ZWJ) next to a word character to the word-character definition, with fixtures, or narrow the 'never replaces a word fragment' clause to the listed categories and record the joiner case as accepted behavior in Clarifications.

citations.excerpt: so a rule never replaces a word fragment, including in Indic scripts (dependent vowel signs, virama) and next to a decomposed (NFD) accent
so that** a rule never corrupts unrelated words

findings.description: The CJK side exemption removes every boundary check, including the new combining-mark rule. A rule ending in a kana followed by a decomposed voiced mark (U+3099, part of the kana set) matches the base kana and leaves the mark on the replacement, which contradicts 'never replaces a word fragment ... next to a decomposed (NFD) accent'.
findings.suggestion: State that a combining mark immediately after the match blocks it on every side, including CJK-exempt sides (equivalently, a match never splits a base character from its following combining marks).

citations.excerpt: On a side where the recognized text begins or ends with a CJK ideograph, kana or hangul character, no boundary check applies, because those scripts are written without spaces.
The side-by-side CJK exemption is unchanged.

findings.description: The exemption is justified by 'written without spaces', yet it covers hangul (Korean separates words with spaces) and excludes Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar and Tibetan, which are written without spaces. In those scripts a rule only matches when the transcript happens to contain spaces or punctuation around it, so rules are mostly inert; for Korean the exemption allows matches inside space-delimited words.
findings.suggestion: Decide explicitly which scripts are exempt and why (word-segmentation need versus particles), name them in AC-006 and add a fixture per decision; at minimum document that rules are inert inside unspaced Thai/Lao/Khmer/Myanmar text.

citations.excerpt: because those scripts are written without spaces

findings.description: Lengths are in 'characters' without naming the unit (Unicode scalar values, UTF-16 units or grapheme clusters), and the normalized key does not mention canonical equivalence, so NFC 'café' and NFD 'café' are two distinct keys that look identical in the list, and a rule typed in one form does not match a transcript in the other.
findings.suggestion: State that lengths count Unicode scalar values and that keys and matching are literal without Unicode normalization (or add NFC normalization of both sides), with one fixture each.
